title: Remember you will die
hookLine: tradition says monks kept skulls on their desks to value each day

cards: A skull on a writing desk, beside the candle and the open book. Tradition says some monks kept one there, not to be gloomy, but to be reminded.
In old paintings a skull sometimes sits beside a saint at prayer, as calm as an inkwell. But the Bible has a prayer that asks for the same reminder, without bones on the desk.
Its heading calls it "A Prayer of Moses the man of God." Today's word is a Latin phrase for what the skull was saying.

teach.h: TEACH US TO NUMBER OUR DAYS.
teach.b: First, the request. Psalm ninety, which day one thousand read for its thousand years, asks: "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom." Not count your years.
Number your days. And it's asked as a lesson, teach us, not handed down as a threat. The point of the counting is a wiser heart.
The same psalm says people are like grass: "In the morning it flourisheth, and groweth up; in the evening it is cut down, and withereth." And: "we spend our years as a tale that is told."
James asks outright: "For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away." Third, the Latin.
Memento mori: remember that you will die. Not a Bible verse, but a saying Christians kept close to the Bible's words. Some churches put it in the body.
On Ash Wednesday, in Catholic and some Protestant churches, a minister marks ashes on the forehead, sometimes with words from Genesis: "for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return."
Other churches don't keep the day. Fourth, why want this? Ecclesiastes says it's better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting, because the living will lay it to heart.
Remembering the end sorts what matters from what doesn't. In this block it sits beside everything else: dust, and all things new. On the desk, the skull sat beside an open book.

how: On Ash Wednesday, Catholic and some Protestant churches mark ashes on the forehead, sometimes with the words 'remember that thou art dust'; some Christians also pray Psalm 90 at funerals or at the turn of the year.

games.why: a reminder, not a threat: "so teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom."

practice: Think of your own death gently for about a minute, your life as a tale that is told; if today is hard for that, or you're grieving, number just this one day.
Then ask what would make today count: a call, an apology, an hour given to someone. If you pray, say teach us to number our days; if not, hold the day in your hands.
If thoughts of death feel heavy or dark, you don't have to carry them alone: call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
